myisam-vs-innodb.title: The same transaction on two engines
myisam-vs-innodb.alt: A recorded run on MySQL with tabs for InnoDB and MyISAM. A session begins a transaction and inserts a row. On InnoDB another session can't see the row, and rollback removes it. On MyISAM the row is visible at once, and rollback does nothing, because MyISAM has no transactions.

variants.label: InnoDB
variants.summary: Isolation and rollback both worked. The row never existed for anyone else.

steps.note: The engine is InnoDB.
Inserted, and not committed.
Session A sees its own row.
Can another connection see it?
Session A changes its mind.
Is it gone?

variants.label: MyISAM
variants.summary: BEGIN and ROLLBACK were accepted and did nothing. The row was visible at once and is still there.

steps.note: The engine is MyISAM.
Inserted, and not committed.
Session A sees its own row.
Can another connection see it?
Session A changes its mind.
Is it gone?

table-lock.title: A MyISAM read holds up a write to any row
table-lock.alt: A recorded run on MySQL. Session A locks a MyISAM table for reading, as a long report does. Session B's update of an unrelated row waits for the whole table. On InnoDB the same update of a different row isn't blocked by a row lock held elsewhere.

variants.label: MyISAM
variants.summary: Locks are per table: session B's row had nothing to do with session A, and it waited anyway.

steps.note: A long report on a MyISAM table holds a table-level read lock. This statement makes that lock last long enough to see.

steps.sql: UPDATE t SET v = 2 WHERE id = 2
steps.note: Session B wants to change a single row. It waits for the whole table.
Only when the report ends does the update go through.

variants.label: InnoDB
variants.summary: Locks are per row: different rows don't get in each other's way.

steps.note: On InnoDB, session A works on row 1.

steps.sql: UPDATE t SET v = 2 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: That locks row 1 only.

steps.sql: UPDATE t SET v = 2 WHERE id = 2
steps.note: Row 2 is free, so this goes straight through.
Done.

cursor-hold.title: An open cursor is a held-open transaction
cursor-hold.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session A opens a cursor inside a transaction and fetches some rows. Session B's ALTER TABLE waits, because the cursor's transaction still holds a lock on the table, until session A commits.

steps.note: A cursor lives inside a transaction.

steps.sql: DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT * FROM grades ORDER BY id
steps.note: The query is planned, and no rows are returned yet.
Three rows. The cursor remembers where it is.

steps.sql: ALTER TABLE grades ADD COLUMN note text
steps.note: A schema change needs an exclusive lock, and the open transaction is holding a lock. It waits. So does everything queued behind it.
The application is in no hurry: it's still paging through.
Closing the transaction closes the cursor, and the ALTER goes through.

blocks.cmd:
-- client side: one query, every row comes back
SELECT id, g, name FROM grades;
blocks.out: 2,000,000 rows in 1541.6 ms, about 365 MB of client memory

blocks.cmd:
-- server side: a cursor, 50 rows at a time
DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT id, g, name FROM grades;
FETCH LAST FROM c;   -- the server has to work through everything
DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT id FROM grades WHERE g BETWEEN 90 AND 100;

cursor.title: A server-side cursor
cursor.hint: This box keeps its transaction open between runs, like a real client would. Run the presets in order. The status line says when a transaction is still open.
cursor.setup:
CREATE TABLE grades (id int, g int, name text);
INSERT INTO grades SELECT g, g % 100, 'student ' || g FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g;
